idiom_name: Record<K, () => T> literal checked with satisfies (Map<K, () => T> for runtime registration)
implementation_notes: A registry keyed by a string-literal union is typed as Record<ShapeKind, () => Shape>, so the compiler proves that every key is present and that no unknown key appears, while the satisfies operator (TypeScript 4.9) checks that literal without widening the properties' precise types - the type-level reading of 'the factory cannot anticipate the types' is that the table cannot omit one either. For an open set, Map<string, () => Shape> with an explicit has() check before get() is the runtime table, and Readonly or Object.freeze keeps the configured kit from drifting. What replaces the classic structure: the object literal (or the Map) plus arrow functions; where the variants are closed, a discriminated union consumed by an exhaustive switch - with a never-typed default branch - needs no keys at all.
pitfalls: Record<string, () => T> is not a checked table: an index signature accepts any key and, without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, tells the compiler the lookup is always defined, so validate keys at run time or keep the key union narrow.
satisfies only checks the literal it is attached to; a table assembled at run time from dynamic keys gets no exhaustiveness, and module-level state is shared across tests and hot reloads.

Typing the table entries as Function or any erases the argument contract, so a builder can be called with the wrong arguments; keep the arrow functions (or constructors) in the table so each key keeps its own parameter list.
